summary: Specifies a data model for handling quotas on accounts for servers using JMAP, so clients can see usage limits.

eli5.summary: A way for a mail program to ask how much space you have left and how much you have used.

questions: how to check mailbox quota with jmap
how do i check my quota with jmap
what is the difference between soft limit and hard limit
subtitle: A JMAP data type that lets a client see how much of its allowance it has used, and where the limits are.

tldr.problem: Clients of a JMAP server have no standard way to learn about the usage limits on their accounts and how close they are to them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9425 adds a Quota data type with usage, warn, soft and hard limits, a scope and a unit of measure, plus the standard JMAP get, changes, query and queryChanges methods and a capability URI to announce support.
tldr.outcome: A client can fetch quotas, track just the changing usage figure efficiently, and receive push notifications. Administering quotas is out of scope.

today: RFC 9425 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2023, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Quota Extension Is For
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP, RFC 8620) is a generic protocol for synchronizing data such as mail, calendars or contacts between a client and a server. It is optimized for mobile and web environments.

This document defines a data model for handling quotas over JMAP, so that a user can obtain details about a certain quota. It does not address quota administration, which should be handled by other means. It reuses the notation and terminology of RFC 8620, and the capitalized term "Quota" means the data type defined in Section 4 and instances of it.
sections.eli5: This lets your mail program read the meter on your storage. It only reads it. Changing how big your locker is happens somewhere else.

sections.title: Scope and Resource Type
sections.content:
Two fields of the Quota type take values from fixed sets.

Scope says who the quota applies to: account (just the client's account), domain (all accounts sharing the domain) or global (all accounts on the server).

ResourceType is the unit of measure for usage: count (a number of objects of a data type, for example a limit of 50 "Mail" objects) or octets (size in octets, for example a limit of 25000 octets).
sections.eli5: Scope is whose locker it is: yours, your class's, or the whole school's. The resource type is whether you count items or measure how heavy they are.

sections.title: The Quota Object
sections.content:
A Quota shows the limit set on an account's usage and the current usage against it. It MUST contain these fields: id, resourceType, used (current usage, computed by the server), hardLimit (objects in scope may not be created or updated once it is reached), scope, name (useful for managing and searching quotas) and types (the JMAP type names, such as Email or Calendar, that the quota applies to).

The server MUST filter out any types for which the client did not request the capability in the using section of the request, and MUST NOT return Quota objects for which the client recognizes no types.

Three fields MAY be present. warnLimit can be used to warn an entity about to reach the hard limit soon, with no action taken yet. softLimit can be used to allow some operations but refuse others, for example blocking outgoing events such as sending email while still receiving incoming ones; what is allowed is up to the server. description is a free, human-readable explanation, encoded in UTF-8 and chosen using the request's Accept-Language header or out-of-band language information. When set, the warn limit SHOULD be lower than the soft limit and the hard limit, and the soft limit SHOULD be higher than the warn limit but lower than the hard limit.
sections.eli5: The meter shows how much you have used and has three marks: a yellow warning line, an orange line where some things stop working, and a red line where it is full.

sections.title: The JMAP Methods
sections.content:
Quota uses the standard JMAP methods from RFC 8620. Quota/get is the standard get, and its ids argument may be null to fetch all quotas of the account at once. Quota/queryChanges is the standard queryChanges method.

Quota/changes is the standard changes method with one extra response argument, updatedProperties. If only used changed since the old state, it is a list containing just that property; if the server cannot tell, it MUST be null. Because used changes often and other properties rarely, this lets a client use a back-reference in a following Quota/get in the same request and fetch only what changed. Servers MAY add other frequently changing properties to the list.

Quota/query is the standard query method. Its filter conditions are name (contains the given string), scope and resourceType (exact match), and type (the types property contains the value). An object matches only if all given conditions match. Sorting MUST be supported on name and used.
sections.eli5: Since the used amount changes all the time and the limits almost never do, the server can say "only the used number changed", so the program does not have to re-read everything.

sections.title: Examples and Push
sections.content:
The RFC's first example sends Quota/get with ids set to null. The response lists a quota with resourceType count, used 1056, warnLimit 1600, softLimit 1800, hardLimit 2000 and scope account, whose description says the user cannot send mails or create contacts and calendar events once the soft limit is reached.

The second example sends Quota/changes and a Quota/get that uses back-references to the /updated and /updatedProperties results. Only used changed, so the returned object holds just id and used (1246).

Servers MUST support the JMAP push mechanisms from RFC 8620 so clients can be notified when the state of the Quota type changes.
sections.eli5: In the examples, the program reads the meter, then later asks "what changed?" and gets back just the new number. The server can also tap the program on the shoulder when the meter moves.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
All security considerations of JMAP apply. Implementations must not violate the site's security policy, and the resource usage of other users is likely to be confidential and should not be disclosed to unauthorized people.

A resource shared across users, such as a quota with domain or global scope, lets one user affect what others can use. For example, a user could spam themselves with events until the shared resource hits its limit; the RFC suggests server-side rate limiting as a mitigation.

Showing domain and global quota counts to everyone can also leak data. By comparing the count before and after a message is sent to a private list, a user could infer how many people are on it. To limit such attacks, quotas with domain or global scope SHOULD only be visible to server administrators and not to general users.
sections.eli5: If everybody can see the meter for the whole school's storage, they can guess secrets from how it moves. So only the principal should see that meter.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the JMAP capability urn:ietf:params:jmap:quota (intended use: common, change controller: IETF) and the JMAP data type Quota, which cannot reference blobs and can be used for state change.

Servers supporting this specification MUST add the capability URI to the capabilities object of the JMAP Session. Its value is an empty object, both in the Session capabilities and in an account's accountCapabilities.
sections.eli5: The extension gets an official name tag, so a client can ask whether the server understands quotas before trying to use them.

viz.caption: THE THREE LIMITS ON A QUOTA

cells: Warn before the hard limit is near; no action taken yet.
Allow some operations but refuse others; server decides which.
Objects in scope may not be created or updated once reached.
